analysis.one_liner: Bans sale of toys and child care products containing certain hormone-disrupting plastic softeners.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate committee it was assigned to; it got no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated any toy or child care article (like teethers or feeding products) containing certain phthalates—chemicals used to soften PVC plastic—as a banned hazardous substance under federal law, starting January 1, 2009. It would also have required manufacturers replacing phthalates to pick the least toxic alternative and barred them from swapping in known carcinogens or reproductive toxicants. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, who would no longer find phthalates in teethers, soft plastic toys, and sleep or feeding products. The bill's own findings cite scientific literature reporting hormone-disrupting effects of phthalates and evidence that humans carry levels associated with adverse effects [S3]. Manufacturers that had already moved to phthalate-free products would also gain a level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: Any children's product or child care article containing DEHP, DBP, or BBP above 0.1 percent would be treated as a banned hazardous substance under the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, making its manufacture and sale illegal [S2] [S3].
For products meant for children under 3 that can be mouthed, the ban extends to additional phthalates (DINP, DIDP, DnOP), covering the products most likely to end up in a baby's mouth [S3].

Manufacturers could not simply swap phthalates for another hazard: replacements had to be the least toxic available, and known carcinogens or EPA-identified reproductive and developmental toxicants were prohibited as alternatives [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Toy and child care product manufacturers using PVC plastic, which would have had to reformulate products and absorb the cost of substitutes, testing, and inventory changes; some of that cost could pass through to retail prices.

drawbacks.text: Reformulation is not free: manufacturers would have borne the cost of finding substitutes, retesting products, and clearing existing inventory, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers in the form of higher prices [S3].

The ban swept in all phthalates above a fixed 0.1 percent threshold for mouthable products for children under 3, including DINP, DIDP, and DnOP, for which the chemical industry argued the health evidence was less conclusive than for DEHP and DBP; a fixed bright-line rule leaves no room for case-by-case safety findings [S3].
The bill's effectiveness depended on enforcement of the Federal Hazardous Substances Act regime, and small importers and toymakers would face the same compliance burden as large ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a well-documented class of hormone-disrupting chemicals in products babies mouth and chew, and it guarded against the obvious loophole of swapping in a known carcinogen. The main cost is one-time reformulation expense for manufacturers, a burden the industry bears regularly when safety rules change. On the substance, the bill was modest and targeted; the real problem was that it never received any consideration.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill in the Senate on October 31, 2007 [S1] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the day it was introduced [S5].
No committee action, floor vote, or further step appears in the action history for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
It had only three cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of phthalate-containing PVC toys and child care products were better off: no reformulation deadline arrived and no compliance costs were imposed. Parents had no federal guarantee that these chemicals were out of children's products under this bill.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it

for.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by Democrats and never reached a vote, so there is no record of how either party would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would have made phthalate-containing children's products illegal to sell, cutting off a major market for these plasticizers. The industry's avoided compliance costs were the public's forgone protection.

industries.industry: Toy and child care product manufacturers
industries.note: Manufacturers would have faced reformulation, testing, and inventory costs. Some toy makers already selling phthalate-free lines would have benefited from uniform rules.
